title: Sorting
short: sort or sorted, by any rule you give with key=.
what: sorted(x) returns a new sorted list; x.sort() sorts the list itself and returns None. key= tells Python what to compare, and a tuple key sorts by one thing, then breaks ties with the next.
analogy: Lining up a class: first by height, and when two kids are the same height, by name. The key is the question you ask each kid.

frames.label: words
frames.say: Four words, in no order. sorted(words) makes a new sorted list and leaves words alone.

frames.label: sorted(words)
frames.say: With no key, strings sort alphabetically: a, f, k, p. Numbers would sort smallest first.

frames.label: sorted(words, key=len)
frames.say: key=len sorts by length. pear and kiwi tie at 4 and keep their old order: Python's sort is stable.

frames.label: key=len, reverse=True
frames.say: reverse=True flips it: longest first. The tie still keeps pear before kiwi.

frames.label: key=lambda w: (len(w), w)
frames.say: key=lambda w: (len(w), w) sorts by length, then A to Z on ties. Tuples compare item by item.

frames.label: key=lambda w: (-len(w), w)
frames.say: Longest first but ties A to Z? Negate the number: (-len(w), w). reverse=True would flip both parts.

frames.label: x = words.sort()
frames.say: words.sort() sorts in place and returns None. x = words.sort() leaves x = None, a common bug.

when: Order by one thing, then another
python:
words = ["pear", "fig", "apple", "kiwi"]
print(sorted(words))
print(sorted(words, key=len))
print(sorted(words, key=len, reverse=True))
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: (len(w), w)))
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: (-len(w), w)))
x = words.sort()
print(x, words)
pairs = [[1, 9], [0, 3], [1, 2]]
pairs.sort()
print(pairs)
print(sorted("dcab"), "".join(sorted("dcab")))
watch: list.sort() returns None. nums = nums.sort() throws your list away.
sorted("dcab") returns a list of characters. Use "".join(sorted(s)) for a string.
reverse=True flips every part of the key. To flip only a number, negate it.
